spec_choices.why: The designer fixed 3 seats. The deal (9 cards plus the 10th as trump), the leader rotation mod 3 and the play order all assume three players. The game is about predicting tricks and managing the trick count against two rivals whose bids are public.

A thoughtful player bids from card strength and the trump suit, then plays to hit the bid exactly: dumping Jesters or low cards to avoid tricks, spending Wizards or trumps to take them, and reading the opponents' public bids to disrupt them. A thoughtless player bids blindly and plays cards in any order.
The source has no table talk, and adding it would add a mechanic.

spec_choices.what: Shuffle and deal written as random draws from the deck list
spec_choices.why: The engine shuffles by drawing at random; drawing 9 cards and then one more for trump matches 'top 3 to each seat, the 10th is trump'.

spec_choices.what: The bid and tricks_taken are public attributes
spec_choices.why: The rules announce bids after the simultaneous poll and announce each trick winner, so both are open information. The poll keeps bids secret until all are in.

simplifications.what: The source's 'draw' when two or three players tie for the top score becomes a shared win
simplifications.why: The engine ranks by one expression and players level at the top share the win; there is no separate draw outcome.

simplifications.what: Each of the three plays is written as three steps (build offer, ask, resolve) addressed to the computed seat
simplifications.why: The engine runs a flat list of steps; play order is expressed by naming the seat from leader.

simplifications.what: Hand-start steps carry a 'when trick_in_hand = 1' condition, and scoring carries 'when trick_in_hand = 3'
simplifications.why: Single steps may be conditional, so no block substitution is needed.

variation.original_summary: Wizard is a trick-taking game for 3-6 players with a 60-card deck (four suits of 1-13, plus 4 Wizards and 4 Jesters). Hands grow from 1 card to 60/players cards, a turned card sets trump, and each player bids the exact number of tricks they will take. An exact bid scores 20 plus 10 per trick, and a missed bid loses 10 per trick off.

review.evidence: Every fixed bid loses. Always bidding 0 fails whenever the hand is strong, and always bidding high fails on weak hands. Missing by k costs 10k, so no fixed policy can match a player who reads their hand. One seat edge exists: bidding in turn order gives the last bidder information. A second, much smaller one comes from leading.

Skill shows in hand evaluation, card counting and dumping or ducking tricks. Single hands are very card-driven, though, and the many tiny early hands are close to lotteries. Skill wins out only over many hands.

A weak player can still score exact bids of 0 or 1. A strong player keeps improving by inferring others' hands from their bids and play, steering tricks to the right player, and playing to make others miss.
Hands are hidden. Bids reveal partial information. Each trick requires inferring what the remaining players hold and planning across the rest of the hand.
Trick winners and scores follow mechanically from the cards played and the bids.

The original runs up to 20 hands of up to 20 cards, which means hundreds of sequential choices. It also needs a 60-card deck, a dealer trump choice, a variable hand size and a sequential bidding order. This exceeds the step and round limits.

problems: P1: Length and size. Variable hands up to 20 cards and up to 60 hands far exceed 40 rounds and 4 choices per round.
P2: Sequential bidding gives the last bidder a built-in information edge, and the dealer's trump choice on a Wizard adds an extra sub-procedure.

P3: The previous build did not offer the bid options 0-3 to seats. It derived them from parameter attributes (bid_min..bid_max) that did not produce a valid option list. Every bid then fell to the default 1, which overwrote valid answers including 0. This broke the deal/bid scenario (R1), the recorded-bids scenario (R3) and the new-hand scenario (R4).

P4: The illegal-choice fallback (lowest led-suit card, else Jester, else lowest suited card with colour tie-breaks, and so on) was a long priority chain. It was built incorrectly (R9) and is error-prone to build.
P5: Tiny one-card hands are nearly pure luck, so card luck swamps skill in early hands.

changes.what: Three players, a 28-card deck (Red, Blue, Green 1-8, plus 2 Wizards and 2 Jesters), 12 hands of exactly 3 cards. Each round is one trick, so there are 36 rounds.
changes.why: This keeps trick-taking, trump and exact bidding within 40 rounds and at most 4 choices per round. Every hand is large enough to plan over.

changes.what: Every hand has 3 cards instead of 1 to 20.
changes.why: Removes the near-random one-card hands. Every hand now offers a real bid decision and in-hand planning.

changes.what: Bids are a single simultaneous poll. The literal fixed options 0, 1, 2 and 3 are written directly into the step, not computed from attributes. The answer is stored exactly as given. The default of 1 applies only if the answer is missing or not one of 0-3. The bid is not touched again until end-of-hand scoring.
changes.why: Simultaneous bidding removes the last-bidder edge. Hard-coding the option list fixes the build failure where no options were offered and every bid became 1.

changes.what: A turned Wizard or Jester simply means no trump.
changes.why: Removes the dealer-choice sub-procedure and the dealer's advantage.

changes.what: The first leader of hand h is seat ((h - 1) mod 3) + 1. After that, the trick winner leads.
changes.why: Balances the leading advantage over 12 hands (4 each).

changes.what: The illegal-choice fallback is one rule: play the first card of the player's legal-card list, which keeps the order the cards sit in their hand.
changes.why: This is a one-operation fallback that is deterministic and easy to build and test, replacing the broken priority chain.

changes.what: Trick resolution uses one numeric strength per card, and the best card is replaced only by a strictly greater strength. A Wizard is 100, a trump is 20 + rank, a led-suit card is its rank, and anything else is 0.
changes.why: Implements 'first Wizard wins, else highest trump, else highest led suit, all Jesters means the first Jester wins' as plain arithmetic, with no lookup table.

keeps: Wizards always win, with the first one played taking the trick. Jesters always lose, and the first one wins only if every card is a Jester.
A turned card sets trump each hand.
Players must follow the led suit if able, but Wizards and Jesters may always be played.
When a Jester is led, the next suited card sets the led suit. When a Wizard is led, there is no led suit.
Exact-bid scoring: 20 + 10 per trick when exact, otherwise -10 per trick off.
Bids need not sum to the number of tricks.
The highest total after the last hand wins.

recommendation.reason: The core of hidden hands, exact bidding and trick inference fits the platform once the game is shrunk to 3 players, 3-card hands and simultaneous bids with a hard-coded option list.

variation.name: Three-Card Wizard
variation.summary: A compact Wizard for 3 players: 12 hands of 3 cards from a 28-card deck, simultaneous exact bids, and one trick per round.
variation.objective: After hand 12, the player with the highest score wins. If two or three players tie for the highest score, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Simultaneous bids remove the last-bidder edge, and rotating the first lead balances the seats. Three-card hands make every bid a real estimate: count Wizards and trumps, and judge how the off-suit cards will play. Mid-hand play rewards inference from the announced bids and the cards seen, such as ducking a trick to stay exact or forcing a trick onto an opponent who bid 0. Simple policies lose: always bidding 0 is beaten by reading the hand, and always bidding 3 misses most hands at -10 to -30. Over 12 hands, skill outweighs the deal. Talk is left out: with only 3 players and public bids, messages would add little beyond the bids and could enable two-player collusion against the third.

balanced.evidence:
BID TABLE. There are 3 tricks among 3 players, so the mean is 1 trick each. For a random 3-card hand played thoughtlessly (always the first card of the offer), I estimate the tricks taken as P(0)≈0.30, P(1)≈0.44, P(2)≈0.21, P(3)≈0.05. Payoff of each bid against tricks taken t (exact = 20+10t, else -10|t-bid|):
  bid 0: t0 +20, t1 -10, t2 -20, t3 -30, EV ≈ 6 - 10.1 = -4.1
  bid 1: t0 -10, t1 +30, t2 -10, t3 -20, EV ≈ 13.2 - 6.1 = +7.1
  bid 2: t0 -20, t1 -10, t2 +40, t3 -10, EV ≈ 8.4 - 11.0 = -2.6
  bid 3: t0 -30, t1 -20, t2 -10, t3 +50, EV ≈ 2.5 - 19.9 = -17.4
No bid is strictly better whatever happens: each bid is the best payoff in its own column. Which bid is best depends on the hand and the trump. A Wizard or a high trump pushes a bid of 1 or 2. Low off-suit cards and Jesters favour 0, and that bid can be defended by ducking.
THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE (highest of three totals after 12 hands wins):
- Always the first option (bid 0, first legal card): about -4 per hand, so about -50 over the game. It loses to a hand-reading bidder, who reaches roughly +15 to +20 per hand. Against random players (random bids average far below 0) it often wins, but it plainly loses to sensible play.
- Always the last option (bid 3): about -17 per hand. It loses to everyone, including random play.
- Always bid 1: about +7 per hand, the strongest thoughtless line. It still trails a player who bids 0 on weak hands and 2 on strong ones and then plays to hit the bid.
- Always play the first legal card: this gives up control over ducking and over-taking, so it misses bids more often.
No policy never loses.
SEAT EDGE. Bidding is a simultaneous poll, so the original game's informational advantage for the last bidder is gone. The first leader rotates and each seat leads exactly 4 of the 12 hands. Later leads go to the trick winner, which is symmetric. Play order within a trick gives the usual positional edge to the last player, but leadership moves, so no fixed seat gains. Every seat can realistically win. Nothing in the game is labelled as a cooperation or dilemma structure, so there is no payoff-ordering claim to falsify.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS.
- The deck is 28 cards: 9 dealt, 1 turned for trump, 18 left. This matches the rule text.
- Trump: a suited card gives its suit; a Wizard or Jester gives 'none'. The dealer's choice is removed, so no extra decision is needed.
- Leader: hands 1-12 follow ((h-1) mod 3)+1; later tricks are led by the trick winner.
- Legal cards: you must follow suit, and Wizards and Jesters are always legal. A fallback covers invalid answers.
I traced the strength resolution through its edge cases:
  (a) Jester led, then R5: the Jester sets best 0; R5 sets led_suit=R with strength 5, which is greater than 0, so R5 wins. Correct.
  (b) Wizard led: wizard_played=true, so no later card sets led_suit. Others may play anything (led_suit is 'none'). 100 is never beaten because the comparison is strict, so the first Wizard wins.
  (c) Led suit equal to trump: 20+rank, consistent.
  (d) Off-suit non-trump: 0. This cannot beat a Jester lead (0 is not greater than 0), but it can only occur once led_suit is set, where it loses anyway.
  (e) All Jesters: impossible with 2 Jesters, but the rule handles it.
Scoring is pure arithmetic on tricks_taken and bid. Ties are a draw.
LIMITS. Choice steps per round: 1 bid poll (conditional on trick_in_hand=1) plus 3 sequential plays = 4, which meets the limit of 4. Rounds 36 ≤ 40. Hidden elements 1 (hands). Random draws: 1 shuffle, only on trick 1. Attributes counted: table hand_number, trick_in_hand, deck, trump_card, trump_suit, leader, led_suit, wizard_played, best_value, best_seat, played_cards = 11; player hand, bid, tricks_taken, played_card, offer, score = 6; total 17 ≤ 20.
STEPS. Deal and reset take about 4 steps with `when` trick_in_hand=1, combining operations. Then trump 1, leader 1, bid poll plus announce 1-2, trick setup 1, and per player offer-build + choice + resolve = 9, then end of trick and scoring 1-2. That is about 17-19, inside 20. It is tight but feasible, because single steps carry multiple operations and per-step `when` conditions; no block-conditional subsequence is needed.
No board, clock, judge, trading or binding promises are used. The bid poll is correctly simultaneous; card play is sequential by design, which is correct for trick-taking.
TALK. There is none, and that is sensible. All interests conflict: each player wants an exact bid and wants the others to miss. Bids are announced publicly, which already provides the information players need, so talk would add only words or unverifiable bluffs.
REPEATED-GAME CHECK. This is not a cooperation game, so there is no late-round betrayal collapse.

triage.reason: The game asks for bids as a numeric choice with no option list, and offers only legal cards when a player plays. The tests are built on matching option strings ('1', '2', '0', '3', an illegal 'B8'), so their answer rules never fired and defaults were used instead. The game's own trace matches the rules: deck 28-9-1=18, 2 cards left in each hand after the first trick, a trump card turned, and a trump suit set.
triage.guidance: For the bidding poll, give each seat a numeric answer (for example seat 1 bids 2, seat 2 bids 0, seat 3 bids 3) instead of options_include matching. The tests for R1 and R4 should not rely on a bid option '1' being offered; let the default answer apply or supply numeric bids, and assert only the counts (deck 18, hand 2 each) and hand_number. For R9, the game offers only legal cards, so an illegal card like B8 cannot be submitted. Test the fallback through a missing or unmatched answer instead: with R2 and another red card in hand and red led, the engine should play R2. Assert only played_card, tricks_taken, bids and scores, not internal lists like offer or fallback_order.

triage.reason: Every failing scenario breaks at the bidding poll. No seat was ever offered the options 0 or 2 that the tests look for, and all bids came out as 0, even though the rules say a missing bid counts as 1. The rules and the tests are consistent; the game file builds the bid poll wrongly.
triage.guidance:
1. Build bidding (rule 3) as one simultaneous poll of all three seats at the start of each hand (trick_in_hand == 1).
2. Its options must be exactly the numbers bid_min..bid_max, which is 0, 1, 2, 3. Use numbers, not strings, and not a free-form value, so a test answering 2 matches the option 2.
3. Write each chosen value straight into the player's public `bid`. If you keep `bid_said`, copy it into `bid` after the poll; do not leave `bid` at its start value of 0.
4. A missing, declined or invalid answer must set `bid` to default_bid (1), not 0.
5. Then check the rest of the hand flow:
   - The deal puts 3 cards in each hand and removes the 10th card as trump, so the deck holds 18 and each hand 2 after the first trick.
   - The first leader is ((hand_number - 1) mod 3) + 1.
   - The fallback for an illegal card follows rule 8 (a) to (d) exactly: lowest led-suit card first, then Jester, then lowest suited card with ties broken R, B, G, then Wizard.

triage.reason: The bidding poll never offered the options 0, 1, 2 and 3 to any seat, so the tests' bid answers never matched. Even the 0 that was sent was overwritten with the default of 1 and later reset to 0, so the bids are not recorded as the rules require. This is a bug in the game file, not in the tests or the rules.
triage.guidance: Make the start-of-hand bid a single simultaneous poll in which every seat is offered exactly the numeric options bid_min..bid_max (0, 1, 2, 3), built from the parameter attributes. Store each answer in that player's `bid` exactly as given. Apply default_bid (1) only when the answer is missing or outside 0-3; a valid 0 must stay 0. Do not reset or overwrite `bid` during the hand; clear it only after the end-of-hand scoring in rule 11. Check that the deal still happens before the poll on trick 1 of each hand, with 3 cards to each seat and the 10th card as trump, so 18 cards remain in the deck after the first trick. Check that the first leader is seat ((hand_number - 1) mod 3) + 1. Check that the illegal-choice fallback follows the a/b/c/d priority from rule 8, with ties broken Red, then Blue, then Green.

triage.reason: The rules are clear and the platform can express them; the failures come from the game file. An invalid bid answer was stored as '0' (bid_said '0', bid 0) instead of being replaced by the default bid of 1. In the trick scenarios the game never offered the scripted, legal cards, so its per-trick setup and offer building do not follow Rules 5 to 7 when a hand is already in progress.
triage.guidance: 1) Bidding (Rule 4): keep the options exactly 0,1,2,3. Do not let a missing or invalid answer fall back to the first option (0). Set the poll's default or fallback to the default_bid attribute (1). If the engine substitutes before your step runs, compare the raw answer with the option list in an `if` and assign default_bid when it is not one of them. A real answer of 0 must stay 0. 2) Run the deal, bidding and first-leader steps only `when` trick_in_hand = starting_trick_in_hand (1). When a scenario starts at trick_in_hand 2 or 3 with given hands, leader and trump_suit, do not re-deal, re-shuffle or overwrite those values. 3) Every round, reset led_suit='none', wizard_played=false, best_value=initial_best_value, best_seat=0 and played_cards=[] before the first card, so stale values never carry over. 4) For each seat in play order (leader, then (leader mod 3)+1, then ((leader+1) mod 3)+1), rebuild that seat's offer from its current hand just before it chooses. Use Rule 7 (cards of led_suit plus Wizards and Jesters if it holds the led suit, otherwise the whole hand, in hand order) and put exactly that list to the player. 5) After the trick, add 1 to best_seat's tricks_taken and set leader = best_seat, so the next trick is led by the winner. 6) Keep every number in the parameter attributes rather than literals.

triage.reason: In the failing scenario every seat's recorded bid answer was '0', which is a valid option. Rule 4 says 0 stays 0, so the game was right to store bid 0. The test never actually submitted a missing or invalid answer: the 'first' default picks option 0, so it expected 1 where the rules require 0.
triage.guidance: Rewrite 'An invalid bid answer becomes a bid of 1' so that seat 1 really gives an invalid bid answer in round 1, for example '5', 'seven' or an empty or missing answer, and is not left to the 'first' default (which answers 0). Then assert seat 1's bid is 1 and the other seats' valid bids are stored exactly as given. Check the bid right after the poll or at the end of the round, not after hand scoring, since Rule 10 resets bids to 0 at the end of trick 3. Add a separate check that a valid answer of '0' stays 0.

triage.reason: In both failing scenarios the game did what the rules say. In the bid scenario seat 1's recorded answer was '0', a legal bid that the rules say stays 0, so expecting 1 is wrong. In the card scenario seat 1 was dealt W2, R6, B5 by a random shuffle, the fallback played W2 (the first card of the offer), and a Wizard wins the trick, so seat 1 getting the trick is correct; the test predicted a winner that the random deal decides.
triage.guidance: 1) Invalid-bid test: make sure the scripted bid answer for the seat is actually invalid (for example '7' or 'x') or missing. Do not let it fall back to the default 'first' option, which is '0'. Then expect bid 1 for that seat. If the move that reaches the game is a legal value such as '0', expect that value to be kept. 2) Invalid-card test: do not start at trick_in_hand = 1, because Rule 1 then reshuffles and redeals and overwrites any given hands. Set given state at trick_in_hand = 2 (or 3) with explicit hands, leader, trump_suit, led_suit 'none' and best_value -1, give one seat an answer that is not in its offer, and work out the trick winner from the first card of that seat's offer list (built in hand order per Rule 7). Do not predict trick winners from cards dealt by a shuffle. Assert on tricks_taken and score, not on scratch values.
